title: p-Block Elements and Their Compounds – II
summary: O, S, Se, Te, Po (ns² np⁴) are the chalcogens. Oxygen is a gas (O2, diatomic) while sulphur is a solid with S8 rings; oxygen forms strong pπ–pπ double bonds. Ozone (O3) is a bent molecule (117°) prepared by passing silent electric discharge through dry O2 (3O2 ⇌ 2O3, ΔH positive); it is a powerful oxidising agent (PbS + 4O3 → PbSO4 + 4O2; 2KI + O3 + H2O → 2KOH + I2 + O2) and it makes mercury lose its meniscus (tailing of mercury: it forms Hg2O which sticks to the glass). The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs UV radiation; CFCs deplete it. Sulphur allotropes: rhombic (α, stable below 369 K) and monoclinic (β). Sulphur dioxide SO2 (S + O2 → SO2 or 4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2) is a colourless, pungent, acidic gas; it is a reducing agent (decolourises acidified KMnO4, reduces Fe^3+ to Fe^2+, bleaches by reduction) and is used for bleaching and making H2SO4. Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the Contact process: S → SO2 → SO3 (V2O5 catalyst, 673–723 K, 2 bar) → H2S2O7 (oleum, in conc. H2SO4) → H2SO4. Conc. H2SO4 is a strong dehydrating agent (turns blue CuSO4·5H2O white, chars sugar), an oxidising agent, and has a low volatility (NaCl + conc. H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl).

F, Cl, Br, I, At (ns² np⁵) are the most reactive non-metals; F2 is the strongest oxidising agent, with oxidising power F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2; fluorine shows only −1 while others show +1, +3, +5, +7 (in oxoacids and interhalogens). Chlorine is prepared by MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O or the Deacon process, and bleaches by oxidation. HCl is prepared from NaCl and conc. H2SO4 at 420 K; it is a strong acid; aqua regia (3 HCl : 1 HNO3) dissolves gold and platinum. Interhalogens (ClF, ClF3, BrF5, IF7) are more reactive than the halogens (except F2). Oxoacids: HOCl < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4 (acid strength increases with oxidation state of Cl).

He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn have completely filled ns² np⁶ shells (He 1s²), very high ionisation enthalpies and positive electron gain enthalpies, so they are very unreactive. Xenon forms compounds with fluorine and oxygen: Xe + F2 → XeF2 (Xe in excess F2 at 673 K), XeF4 (1:5, 873 K) and XeF6 (1:20, 573 K, 60–70 atm). Hydrolysis: XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF; XeF6 + 2H2O → XeOF4 + 2HF (partial); 6XeF4 + 12H2O → 4Xe + 2XeO3 + 24HF + 3O2. Shapes: XeF2 linear, XeF4 square planar, XeF6 distorted octahedral, XeO3 trigonal pyramidal, XeOF4 square pyramidal. Uses: He in balloons and diving gas mixtures, Ne in discharge tubes, Ar in welding and bulbs, Kr/Xe in lamps.

objective: (a) Which gas makes mercury lose its meniscus? (b) Write the formula of the compound formed.
(a) Ozone. (b) Mercury(I) oxide, Hg2O (sticks to glass).
April 2026
Complete and balance: (a) XeF6 + 2H2O → ______ (b) NaCl + conc. H2SO4 (423 K) → ______.
(a) XeOF4 + 2HF. (b) NaHSO4 + HCl.
October 2024
Fill in: (a) The catalyst in the Contact process is ______. (b) The shape of XeO3 is ______.
(a) V2O5. (b) trigonal pyramidal.
State true or false: (a) SO2 acts as a reducing agent. (b) Oxygen shows an oxidation state of +6 like sulphur.
(a) True. (b) False – oxygen shows −2 (and −1, +2 in OF2); it has no +6 state.

vsa: Explain why mercury loses its meniscus (tailing) in contact with ozone.
Ozone oxidises mercury to mercury(I) oxide (2Hg + O3 → Hg2O + O2), which dissolves in mercury and sticks to glass, so the meniscus is lost.
April 2026
Why is SO2 a reducing agent? Give a reaction.
In SO2 sulphur is in +4 state and can be oxidised to +6. It decolourises acidified KMnO4: 5SO2 + 2MnO4− + 2H2O → 5SO4^2− + 4H+ + 2Mn^2+.
April 2026
Write the reaction of XeF6 with water giving XeO3 and state the shape of XeO3.
XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF. XeO3 is trigonal pyramidal with sp³ hybridisation (one lone pair).
April 2026
How does ozone act as an oxidising agent? Give an example.
Ozone readily gives up an oxygen atom (O3 → O2 + [O]). PbS + 4O3 → PbSO4 + 4O2; it also liberates iodine from KI.
April 2025
Why does sulphur dioxide behave as a reducing agent while sulphur trioxide does not?
In SO2 sulphur has the oxidation state +4 (can rise to +6); in SO3 sulphur is already in its highest state +6 and can only be reduced.
April 2025
Why are noble gases chemically inert?
They have completely filled valence shells (ns² np⁶), very high ionisation enthalpies and positive electron gain enthalpies.
Write the reaction for the preparation of chlorine from HCl and MnO2.
MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O.
What are interhalogen compounds? Give two examples.
Compounds formed between two different halogens, e.g. ClF3 and IF7.
sa: Describe the manufacture of sulphuric acid by the Contact process with the reactions.

Steps: S + O2 → SO2; SO2 is purified and oxidised: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 over V2O5 at 673–723 K and 2 bar; SO3 is absorbed in conc. H2SO4 to give oleum (SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7) and diluted with water: H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4.
Explain the oxidising and dehydrating properties of concentrated sulphuric acid with examples.
Oxidising: Cu + 2H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O; C + 2H2SO4 → CO2 + 2SO2 + 2H2O. Dehydrating: it removes water from blue vitriol (CuSO4·5H2O → white CuSO4) and chars sugar (C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O).
Write the preparation, structure and reaction with water of XeF6.
Xe + 3F2 → XeF6 at 573 K and 60–70 atm. Structure: distorted octahedral (sp³d³). Hydrolysis: XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF, partial hydrolysis gives XeOF4.
Compare the oxidising power and oxidation states of the halogens.
Oxidising power decreases F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 (F2 displaces the others from their halides). Fluorine shows only −1; Cl, Br and I show −1, +1, +3, +5 and +7 in oxoacids and interhalogens.
Explain the ozone layer depletion and its harmful effects.

Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV radiation. CFCs release Cl atoms which convert O3 into O2 in a chain reaction (Cl + O3 → ClO + O2). The thinning of the layer causes skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and plankton.
How is hydrogen chloride prepared in the laboratory? Why is it called a strong acid?
NaCl + H2SO4 (conc.) → NaHSO4 + HCl at 420 K (and at higher temperature Na2SO4). In water it ionises completely: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−, hence a strong acid.
la: (a) Explain SO2 as a reducing agent with two reactions. (b) Describe the preparation of XeO3 and its structure.

(a) 5SO2 + 2KMnO4 + 2H2O → K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 2H2SO4 (purple colour discharged); SO2 + 2Fe^3+ + 2H2O → SO4^2− + 4H+ + 2Fe^2+. Sulphur is oxidised from +4 to +6.
(b) XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF; XeO3 is a colourless explosive solid, trigonal pyramidal (sp³ with one lone pair).
(a) Give the preparation of ozone and write two reactions showing its oxidising property. (b) State two uses of ozone.

(a) Silent electric discharge through dry oxygen: 3O2 → 2O3. Oxidising reactions: PbS + 4O3 → PbSO4 + 4O2; 2KI + H2O + O3 → 2KOH + I2 + O2; it also converts Hg to Hg2O (tailing).
(b) Sterilisation of drinking water and bleaching of oils and waxes.
(a) Compare the properties of F, Cl, Br and I in oxidising power, bond enthalpy and electronegativity. (b) Write the oxoacids of chlorine in increasing order of acidic strength with reasons.

(a) Electronegativity and oxidising power decrease from F to I; the bond enthalpy of Cl–Cl (243 kJ mol^-1) exceeds that of F–F (158) due to lone-pair repulsion in the small F2 and then decreases to I2 (151).
(b) HOCl < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4: increasing oxidation state of Cl and number of oxygens stabilise the anion by resonance.
(a) Describe the xenon fluorides with conditions of preparation and shapes. (b) Write the hydrolysis of XeF4 and XeF6. (c) State two uses of noble gases.

(a) XeF2 (Xe : F2 = 2 : 1, 673 K) linear; XeF4 (1 : 5, 873 K, 7 bar) square planar; XeF6 (1 : 20, 573 K, 60–70 bar) distorted octahedral.
(b) 6XeF4 + 12H2O → 4Xe + 2XeO3 + 24HF + 3O2; XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF.
(c) He is used in balloons and for diving (with oxygen); Ar for an inert atmosphere in welding and in electric bulbs.
